title: Yashoda's rope, two fingers short
hook: a mother can't tie up her son, until he lets her
carry: sadhana: practice uncovers a love already there
tomorrow: a servant's boy eats the sages' leftovers, and something wakes. what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, King Prithu asked for ten thousand ears, and Rupa said pure bhakti makes even liberation look light. But if the love is the point, why practice at all? A mother in Vraja answers.

Early morning in Gokul, in the Bhagavata Purana. Yashoda is churning butter and nursing baby Krishna when the milk on the stove boils over. She sets him down and runs. He is furious. He cracks the churning pot with a stone, eats the fresh butter in secret, slips off, and feeds the butter to the monkeys. She comes back with a stick. He runs; she catches him, and decides to tie him to the big wooden mortar. The rope is two fingers too short. She knots on another. Still two fingers short. Every rope in the house, the same two fingers. She's sweating now, flowers slipping from her hair. And seeing how hard his mother is trying, Krishna lets himself be tied. That's why one of his names is Damodara: the one with a rope around his belly.
screen: `THE CHURNING POT, BROKEN.` → `TWO FINGERS SHORT. AGAIN.` → `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.`

segments.voice: Rupa calls the work of devotion sadhana bhakti, devotion as practice, done with the senses. Then he says something surprising. Bhava, the deeper love, is eternally real. What practice achieves is its showing up in the heart. A window cleared, not a light manufactured. Many teachers read Yashoda's rope this way. Her effort was real, and it mattered. But the last two fingers were never hers to close. Rupa splits practice in two. Vaidhi: practice by rule, because scripture asks, which carries a person on gray mornings when the feeling isn't there. And raganuga: practice that follows the longing of Vraja's people, Yashoda and the cowherds, who never checked a rulebook. One starts from instruction, the other from attraction. Rupa keeps both. And under every rule he sets a verse he quotes from the Padma Purana. In paraphrase: always remember Vishnu; never forget him. Every rule serves those two. That's why, in the month of Kartik, many Krishna devotees light a small lamp to Damodara each evening and sing to the boy with the rope. A rule, yes. And a mother's love, followed.
screen: `SADHANA: IT UNCOVERS, NOT BUILDS.` · `VAIDHI: PRACTICE BY RULE.` · `RAGANUGA: PRACTICE BY LONGING.` · then, large: `REMEMBER, AND NEVER FORGET.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small lamp, light it, the way devotees do for Damodara in Kartik. If you pray, offer it to Krishna and say his name once, softly. If you don't, say one name you never want to forget. Then breathe, and each time your mind wanders off, say the name again, gently, without scolding yourself. The effort is yours. Let the rest come.
Rupa Goswami's Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu: a book in which practice, by rule or by longing, clears a window onto a love already real.
screen: `RUPA GOSWAMI'S BHAKTI RASAMRITA SINDHU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Pocket this: sadhana, practice, uncovers a love already there. Yashoda tied the knots; love closed the gap. Back here tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1669 COUNTS.` → `RUPA'S OCEAN · 5 OF 7.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT WOKE IN THE SERVANT'S BOY?`

howItsDone: In Gaudiya Vaishnava practice, devotees keep daily disciplines such as chanting Krishna's names and hearing the Bhagavata, understood as ways of remembering him. In the month of Kartik, many offer a lamp to Krishna as Damodara each evening. Teachers speak of both practice by rule and practice that follows the longing of Vraja.

fork.setup: you're on team rule: practice because scripture asks, every day. now give the other side its best case. why follow longing instead?
options: it starts from attraction, following the love of Vraja's people toward Krishna.
it lets you skip practice on the days you're not in the mood.
it's the only kind of practice Rupa actually accepts.
fork.reveal: Raganuga follows the spontaneous longing of the people of Vraja. It isn't a pass to skip, and Rupa honors practice by rule too.

original.note: Sanskrit sadhana, the means or practice; Rupa's sadhana bhakti is devotion done as practice.

chat.says: Diya says if you don't FEEL it, practice doesn't count. nani says just show up at 7. who's right?

chat.meaning: Rupa honors practice by rule and practice by longing. Either way, practice uncovers a love he calls already real, like Yashoda's effort meeting Krishna's love.

tie.story: Yashoda's rope kept coming up two fingers short until, seeing how hard she tried, Krishna let himself be tied.

sadhana bhakti.meaning: devotion done as practice, with the senses

bhava.meaning: the deeper love for Krishna that practice brings into view

vaidhi.meaning: practice by rule, because scripture asks for it

raganuga.meaning: practice that follows the spontaneous longing of Vraja's people

Vraja.meaning: Krishna's cowherd village in the stories

Padma Purana.meaning: a Sanskrit scripture Rupa quotes on remembering Vishnu

Damodara.meaning: Krishna with a rope (dama) around his belly (udara)

Kartik.meaning: an autumn month when many devotees offer lamps to Damodara

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.9 (Yashoda binds Krishna to the mortar; the rope is two fingers short, about 10.9.15; seeing her effort, he lets himself be bound, about 10.9.18)

Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.2.5 (sadhana bhakti is of two kinds, vaidhi and raganuga)
Bhakti Rasamrita Sindhu 1.2.8, quoting the Padma Purana (always remember Vishnu, never forget him; all rules and prohibitions serve these two)
